title: Kotlin Basics
description: Modern Kotlin: variables, null safety, collections and data classes.

steps.title: Why Kotlin?
steps.body:
Kotlin is a modern, **concise** and **safe** language. It is the preferred language for **Android** and also runs on the **JVM**, on servers and in multiplatform projects.

It fully interoperates with Java.

steps.title: The main function
steps.body:
Every Kotlin program starts at **fun main()**. Statements go inside curly braces, and **println()** prints a line of text.

Semicolons are optional, so most lines have none.

steps.title: Hello, Kotlin

notes.text: fun declares a function, and main is the entry point.
println prints text and moves to a new line.
print does not add a newline.
This text continues the previous line.

steps.title: Arithmetic

notes.text: Multiplication binds tighter than addition.
Dividing two Ints gives an Int, so the fraction is dropped.
If one side is a Double, the result is a Double.
% gives the remainder.

steps.question: What does println(7 / 2) display in Kotlin?
steps.explanation: Int division drops the fraction, so the result is 3.

steps.question: Which declaration is the entry point of a Kotlin program?
steps.explanation: Kotlin programs start at fun main().

steps.title: val and var
steps.body: Use **val** for values that never change (read-only) and **var** for variables you can reassign. Prefer **val** by default; it makes code easier to reason about.

steps.title: Type inference and templates
steps.body:
Kotlin **infers** types from the value: 42 is an Int and "hi" is a String. You can also write types explicitly, like **val pi: Double = 3.14**.

String **templates** embed values using **$name** or **${expression}**.

steps.title: val and var in action

notes.text: val cannot be reassigned.
var can change later.
We update version to 3.
A template inserts both values into the string.

steps.title: Templates and types
steps.code:
fun main() {
    val a = 6
    val b = 4
    println("Sum: ${a + b}")
    println("Product: ${a * b}")
    val pi: Double = 3.14
    println(pi)
}

notes.text: ${ } evaluates any expression inside a string.
The product of 6 and 4 is 24.
An explicit type is optional but allowed.

What happens with this code?
steps.explanation: A val cannot be reassigned, so the compiler rejects the second line.

steps.question: What does this print?
steps.explanation: The template inserts the value of name.

steps.title: Nullable types
steps.body: By default a type **cannot** hold null. Add a question mark, as in **String?**, to allow it. The compiler forces you to handle null before using the value, which removes a whole class of crashes.

steps.title: Safe calls and elvis
steps.body:
The **safe call ?.** only continues when the value is not null. The **elvis operator ?:** supplies a fallback.

The **!!** operator asserts non-null and throws if you are wrong, so use it rarely.

steps.title: Safe calls
steps.code:
fun main() {
    var name: String? = "Kotlin"
    println(name?.length)
    name = null
    println(name?.length)
    println(name ?: "unknown")
}

notes.text: The ? makes the type nullable.
name is not null, so length is 6.
The safe call returns null instead of crashing.
Elvis supplies a default when the left side is null.

steps.title: Conversions that may fail
steps.code:
fun main() {
    val text: String? = null
    val size = text?.length ?: 0
    println(size)
    val num = "42".toIntOrNull()
    val bad = "abc".toIntOrNull()
    println(num)
    println(bad)
}

notes.text: Combine ?. and ?: to get a safe default.
toIntOrNull returns an Int? instead of throwing.
Text that is not a number gives null.

steps.question: Which type can hold null?
steps.explanation: A trailing question mark makes a type nullable.

steps.question: What does this print?
steps.explanation: s is null, so the elvis operator returns the fallback.

steps.question: What does the !! operator do?
options: Throws if the value is null
steps.explanation: !! throws a NullPointerException when the value is null.

steps.title: if is an expression
steps.body: In Kotlin **if** returns a value, so you can write **val x = if (a > b) a else b**. There is no ternary operator because if already does the job.

steps.title: when and ranges
steps.body:
**when** replaces long if-else chains. Branches can match values, several values, ranges and types.

Ranges like **1..5** include both ends, while **1 until 5** excludes the end. Use **for** and **while** for loops.

steps.title: if as an expression

notes.text: score is 85.
The whole if chain produces a String stored in grade.

steps.title: when expression

notes.text: 1..4 includes 4.
when returns a value from the matching branch.
Several values can share one branch.
else handles everything else.

steps.title: Loops

notes.text: A for loop over a closed range.
downTo counts backwards.
while repeats until the condition is false.

steps.question: How many times does for (i in 1 until 4) run?
steps.explanation: until excludes the end value, so i is 1, 2 and 3.

steps.question: What does when return when used as an expression?
options: The value of the matching branch
steps.explanation: As an expression, when evaluates to the matching branch value and must be exhaustive.

steps.title: Lists, sets and maps
steps.body:
Kotlin has **List**, **Set** and **Map**. Create read-only versions with **listOf**, **setOf** and **mapOf**, and changeable ones with **mutableListOf** and friends.

Maps are written with **key to value** pairs.

steps.title: Functional helpers
steps.body:
Collections have powerful helpers: **map** transforms every item, **filter** keeps matches, **sum**, **sorted**, **any** and **all** summarize them.

In a lambda the single parameter is called **it**.

steps.title: Working with a list

notes.text: listOf creates a read-only list.
sorted returns a new ordered list.
map applies the lambda to each item.

steps.title: Mutable lists and maps
steps.code:
fun main() {
    val items = mutableListOf("a", "b")
    items.add("c")
    println(items)
    val ages = mapOf("Ann" to 30, "Bob" to 25)
    println(ages["Ann"])
    println(ages["Zed"])
}

notes.text: A mutable list can grow.
add appends at the end.
to builds key-value pairs.
A missing key gives null.

steps.title: filter and sum

notes.text: filter keeps items where the lambda is true.
sum adds the remaining numbers.
any checks whether at least one item matches.

steps.question: Which function creates a list you can add items to?

steps.title: Declaring functions
steps.body:
Use **fun**, a name, typed parameters and a return type. A single expression can use **=** instead of braces.

Parameters can have **default values** and be passed by **name**.

steps.title: Data classes
steps.body:
A **data class** is a compact holder for data. The compiler writes **toString**, **equals**, **hashCode** and **copy** for you.

Properties are declared in the constructor with **val** or **var**.

steps.title: Functions

notes.text: An expression-bodied function.
greeting has a default value.
5 squared is 25.
Uses the default greeting.
Positional argument overrides the default.

steps.title: Data classes
steps.code:
data class User(val name: String, val age: Int)

fun main() {
    val u = User("Ada", 36)
    println(u)
    val older = u.copy(age = 37)
    println(older.age)
    println(u == User("Ada", 36))
}

notes.text: One line declares the class and its properties.
toString is generated automatically.
copy creates a changed duplicate.
equals compares property values.

steps.question: What does a data class generate automatically?
steps.explanation: Data classes get toString, equals, hashCode, copy and componentN functions.

steps.question: What is the main benefit of a default parameter value?
steps.explanation: Callers may leave out arguments that have defaults.
